subtitle: From a sample to a statement about the population, with an honest measure of how wrong we might be.

est.body:
You cannot ask every voter, test every bulb or weigh every apple. So you measure a few, and you make a claim about all. A statistic computed from a sample estimates a population parameter: x̄ for μ, s² for σ² (÷(n − 1) makes it unbiased), p̂ for p.

What makes an estimator good? It is unbiased (right on average) and has small standard error σ/√n, so more data tightens it. Why divide by n − 1 in the sample variance? Because deviations are measured from x̄, not from the true mean, which makes them a little too small, and n − 1 corrects exactly for that.
keynotes: A statistic computed from a sample estimates a population parameter: x̄ for μ, s² for σ² and p̂ for p.
Dividing by n − 1 makes the sample variance unbiased.
A good estimator is unbiased and has small standard error σ/√n, so more data tightens it.

ci.body:
A single guess is rarely right. A confidence interval gives a range instead, and an honest statement of doubt. With σ known (or n large): x̄ ± z·σ/√n, where z = 1.645, 1.96, 2.576 for 90 %, 95 %, 99 %. Here is the subtle meaning: if you repeated the whole sampling many times, about 95 % of the intervals built this way would contain μ. It is not a 95 % chance that μ lies in one given interval.

Below, 100 simulated intervals at z = 1.96 caught the true mean 96% of the time; at z = 2.576 99% (wider, half-width 5.152 vs 3.92). Rose intervals miss. Work one: n = 25, x̄ = 52, σ = 10. Standard error = 10/5 = 2, so the 95 % half-width = 1.96 × 2 = 3.92, and the interval is 52 ± 3.92. To halve the width of an interval you need four times as much data.
keynotes: With σ known (or n large) the interval is x̄ ± z·σ/√n, where z = 1.645, 1.96, 2.576 for 90 %, 95 %, 99 %.
95 % means about 95 % of intervals built this way would contain μ; it is not a 95 % chance that μ lies in one given interval.
For n = 25, x̄ = 52 and σ = 10 the standard error is 2 and the interval is 52 ± 3.92.

n.body:
Can you have narrow, certain and cheap all at once? No, and here is the formula that proves it. Width = 2zσ/√n. Raising confidence raises z, which makes the interval wider. Raising n shrinks it: the half-width is 3.92 at n = 25 but 1.96 at n = 100, four times the data for half the width.

Precision, confidence and cost pull against each other; you choose two. So raising confidence from 95 % to 99 % with n fixed makes the interval wider.
keynotes: Width = 2zσ/√n: raising confidence raises z and widens the interval.
Raising n shrinks it: the half-width is 3.92 at n = 25 but 1.96 at n = 100.
Precision, confidence and cost pull against each other.

ht.body:
Think of a courtroom. The accused is presumed innocent until the evidence says otherwise. Hypothesis testing works the same way. State a null hypothesis H₀ (“nothing special”, e.g. μ = μ₀) and an alternative H₁. Compute a test statistic, e.g. z = (x̄ − μ₀)/(σ/√n). If it falls in the rejection region (|z| > 1.96 at α = 0.05, two-sided), equivalently if the p-value < α, reject H₀.

Two things can go wrong, and you should name them. Type I = rejecting a true H₀ (probability α), convicting an innocent person. Type II = failing to reject a false H₀ (probability β; power = 1 − β), letting a guilty one go. The decision procedure is the flow in the figure.
keynotes: State a null hypothesis H₀ and an alternative H₁, compute a test statistic such as z = (x̄ − μ₀)/(σ/√n), and reject H₀ if |z| > 1.96 at α = 0.05 (two-sided), equivalently if the p-value < α.
Type I is rejecting a true H₀ (probability α); Type II is failing to reject a false H₀ (probability β; power = 1 − β).
Think of a courtroom: H₀ is presumed innocence, a Type I error convicts the innocent and a Type II error lets the guilty go.

ztest.body:
Let’s try one together. A maker claims a bulb lasts 1000 h (σ = 80). A sample of 64 averages 980 h. Is the claim still believable at α = 0.05? State H₀: μ = 1000 and H₁: μ ≠ 1000. The standard error SE = 80/√64 = 10. The test statistic is z = (980 − 1000)/10 = −2.

Now decide: |z| = 2 exceeds 1.96, so reject H₀ (p ≈ 0.046). With a p-value of 0.03 at α = 0.05, you would reject H₀ as well, since 0.03 is smaller than 0.05. The sample is too far from the claim to be an accident.
keynotes: A maker claims a bulb lasts 1000 h (σ = 80); a sample of 64 averages 980 h.

t.body:
In real life you rarely know σ; you have to estimate it from the same small sample, and that costs you something. Use t = (x̄ − μ₀)/(s/√n) with n − 1 degrees of freedom. The t distribution has heavier tails than the normal, so critical values are larger (2.262 at 9 d.f. vs 1.96), which is the price of not knowing σ. As n grows, t → z.

And for two proportions or categorical counts the χ² test compares observed and expected counts: χ² = Σ(O − E)²/E. A t-test on 12 observations has 12 − 1 = 11 degrees of freedom.
keynotes: When σ must be estimated by s, use t = (x̄ − μ₀)/(s/√n) with n − 1 degrees of freedom.
The t distribution has heavier tails than the normal, so critical values are larger (2.262 at 9 d.f. vs 1.96); as n grows, t → z.
The χ² test compares observed and expected counts: χ² = Σ(O − E)²/E.
